title: Derive a leftmost binary-search boundary
sources: Python 3.14.8 Standard Library: bisect.bisect_left partition contract
Cornell University CS 2112: Loop Invariants, binary-search reasoning (reviewed 2026-10-03)
masterChecklist: Problem decomposition, specifications, preconditions/postconditions, invariants, and proofs by reasoning
Searching, sorting, hashing, heaps, trees, graphs, shortest paths, traversals, union-find, tries
whyItMatters: Copying a binary-search loop is easy; changing a boundary by one can silently skip the first matching record. The loop invariant explains why each update is safe.
simpleExplanation: For a nondecreasing list, a lower bound is the first position whose value is at least the target. It is also the insertion position before equal values. Keep a half-open candidate interval `[lo, hi)`. Everything before `lo` is known to be smaller than the target; everything from `hi` onward is known to be at least the target. If the middle item is too small, discard it and the left half with `lo = mid + 1`. Otherwise keep the middle as a possible first match and set `hi = mid`. The interval shrinks until `lo == hi`, which is the boundary. In everyday code, use the tested standard-library `bisect_left`; writing the loop here teaches the reasoning.
mentalModel: Imagine a sorted row of cards. Two fingers surround the only region where the first card meeting the target could still be. Each comparison moves one finger inward without discarding a possible answer.
outcomes: Explain the half-open `[lo, hi)` candidate interval.
Prove why each branch preserves the lower-bound partition.
Test empty, duplicate, before-first and after-last cases.

realWorldExample.scenario: A study timeline needs the first completion date on or after a requested day.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: An off-by-one error can skip the first matching date or read beyond the list when the requested day is after every item.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Use `bisect_left` in production, define the sorted-date contract, test all boundary cases, and use the derived loop as a learning and review exercise.

workedExample.code:
from bisect import bisect_left

def left_boundary(values, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(values)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if values[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

scores = [40, 55, 55, 80]
print(left_boundary(scores, 55))
print(left_boundary(scores, 60))
print(left_boundary(scores, 100))
assert left_boundary(scores, 55) == bisect_left(scores, 55)
explanation: The input precondition is nondecreasing order under the same comparison rule.
Initially `[lo, hi)` covers every element whose comparison is still unknown; the final insertion position is allowed to be len(values).
When values[mid] is below target, every earlier value is also below target, so the first valid position must be after mid.
Otherwise mid may be the first valid position, so the right boundary becomes mid rather than mid - 1.
Each loop makes the candidate interval smaller. At equality, lo is the first index with value at least target, or len(values) if none exists.
The standard-library assertion checks one example; the invariant argument and wider tests support the general design.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Change `hi = mid` to `hi = mid - 1` and test duplicates. Explain which possible answer was discarded.

procedure: Specify that input values are sorted in nondecreasing order.
Define the desired postcondition: all values before the result are below target and all values at/after it are at least target.
Initialize lo=0, hi=len(values) and state the known partitions.
Check the too-small branch and the candidate-retaining branch separately.
Show termination because hi-lo strictly decreases while positive.
At lo==hi, connect the invariant to the postcondition.
Compare against bisect_left across empty, duplicate and edge cases; use the library function in production unless custom logic is required.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the loop on unsorted data.
commonMistakes.why: The branch cannot safely discard half the candidates.
commonMistakes.avoid: Establish and maintain the sorted-input precondition.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting hi = mid - 1 in this half-open lower-bound pattern.
commonMistakes.why: mid may itself be the first qualifying position.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use hi = mid in the not-too-small branch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the returned position proves equality.
commonMistakes.why: A lower bound is an insertion point even when target is absent.
commonMistakes.avoid: Check index < len(values) and values[index] == target for membership.

assessment.question: What must be true of values before this lower-bound search?
assessment.answer: It must be sorted in nondecreasing order under the same comparison rule.
assessment.explanation: Only then can a midpoint comparison safely discard a region.

assessment.question: What does the result mean when it equals len(values)?
assessment.answer: No item is at least the target; the insertion point is after all items.
assessment.explanation: The result is a boundary, not necessarily an existing item.

assessment.question: Why does the loop terminate?
assessment.answer: Each iteration strictly reduces the positive size of the candidate interval.
assessment.explanation: When lo == hi, the invariant identifies the boundary.
